Dispatch Lab / Deployment and the service lifecycle / 14 September 2026

What it takes to keep a plant operating

Capacity has to arrive, work consumes finite resources, and a completed procedure still needs evidence. Release 2 makes that lifecycle explicit in the plant, its costs and its explanations.

Deployment and maintenance share a physical chronology

Sites now reveals an optional deployment and maintenance design. Work packages carry dependencies, finite project-crew time, access restrictions, acceptance, rework and departure. Only accepted fractions of the plant become available. Construction costs have dates; temporary equipment does not silently become a permanent asset.

Solar ageing and PEM operating exposure are explicit, reduced hypotheses. Delayed, noisy condition readings support four maintenance rules: none, periodic, observed threshold and a forecast-window rule. Replacement requires isolation, compatible support and a spare. Stock, upstream supply, retries and unfinished work persist across saved checkpoints.

Project work and existing field missions cannot occupy the same target concurrently. This conservative exclusion includes a mission’s return. It can delay or expire a job; it is not a globally optimal workforce or fleet scheduler. The additional project crew is separate from the existing field-service crew.

Four new interactive Model essays explain deployment, condition, hardware capabilities and maintenance comparisons. Recorded component links open the original calculation. The main plant illustration, solar illustration and quiet simulation presentation are preserved.

The new mechanisms are opt-in. These are scheduling and observation models with scoped assumptions. No arbitrary robot capability, universal repair probability, remaining-life oracle or certified commissioning is implied.

Fourteen families, with enforceable boundaries

Five families have bounded implementations, one has a human replacement baseline, two use declared assisted work packages, and six remain evidence-restricted. Declaring prerequisites does not make an unsupported mechanism executable. An entry names a model scope; it does not assert that a commercial machine can carry out that task at this plant.

Compare the same plant at more than one boundary

The programme contains 72 seasonal cases across nine saved European weeks, four rules over the same continuous London deployment year, 28 declared uncertainty challenges and 12 archived-forecast cases across three process controllers. Each matched pair shares its environment, initial condition, sensor seed and non-policy assumptions.

The seasonal and annual design cases use saved 2025 ERA5 reanalysis and explicitly labelled previous-day persistence forecasts. They are not measured site data or operational forecast archives. The separate 72-hour Seville controller study uses the original saved ECMWF forecast issues with their availability boundaries.

This is the second execution edition. The first completed all 72 seasonal cases, then paused after 1,337 annual hours when profiling exposed repeated checkpoint encoding. The corrected source is rerun from its starting states. Its 24-hour compatibility check and paired original-state repeats preserve complete physical, observation, service and lifecycle records. The first edition remains separate evidence; its unexecuted cases are not counted as results here.

The short-week fixture deliberately starts near a maintenance threshold: twenty PV years and 45,000 PEM operating hours. The annual fixture commissions a declared previously used plant with two PV years and 38,000 PEM operating hours. These are exposure challenges, not measured asset ages or a proposed maintenance schedule.

Interpret the value of service through its bottleneck
The periodic rule is deliberately due at H168 in the short-window protocol. Those runs end before it can act: its identical weekly output and cost are an unexposed control, not evidence that preventive maintenance has no value. The continuous annual cases use a 4,380-hour interval and exercise that rule across due dates. The interactive teaching comparison also exercises shorter due dates.
In the Seville January week, seed 42, the condition rule initially produced 27.4 kg less methane at 24 hours. By 168 hours it produced 172.6 kg more, after 2 confirmed replacement procedures. Its lifecycle expenditure was €627,240 higher. More output alone does not justify that wholesale replacement assumption. Cases case-002 and case-006.
In the Seville April week, seed 7, the forecast-window rule produced 20.0 kg less methane by 168 hours, but ended with 57.4 kg of hydrogen versus 20.9 kg in the baseline. Stored hydrogen is not methane output. Both batteries were depleted and both reactors were below production temperature at that boundary. A longer continuation could value those states differently; this report assigns no speculative sale proceeds. Cases case-009 and case-015.
Whole-asset replacement is a lumped condition reset with declared work hours. It does not simulate removing and reinstalling every PV module or a complete electrolyser maintenance procedure. The 2–12 hour challenge settings are test inputs, not an established feasible range. The assumed condition channel and these work abstractions need equipment and site evidence before their results support a field recommendation.
Extra solar efficiency may have little production value when the hydrogen buffer is full, CO₂ is limiting, the reactor cannot remain hot, or a work package is still unavailable. A replacement may improve later output while losing production during isolation. Read the physical trajectory and terminal reserves before assigning the difference to “better autonomy”.
The four maintenance rules are heuristics. Selecting economic MPC changes the process-dispatch objective; it does not turn an external replacement threshold into a joint capital or fleet optimiser. These experiments can expose poor rules as well as useful ones.
Allocated costs, dispatch contribution and modelled cash expenditure answer different questions. Opening and replenishment stock are purchases; parts consumed share the existing wear/calendar allowance through a maximum, rather than being charged again on top. Construction replaces the corresponding installation allowance and is excluded from dispatch incentives. No ending inventory receives speculative sale proceeds.
The full-year cash view uses the actual chronological lifecycle year. It refuses to recycle that year into a fictitious twenty-year ageing path. Missing land, logistics, service or commercial inputs remain missing; no profitability or fuel-acceptance claim fills those gaps. The full-array replacement parts use existing illustrative capital assumptions, including €500,000 for solar and €126,000 for the PEM stack at the reference scale.
Condition is an assumption with a scope
The solar starting rate is a reduced linear 0.5% per year hypothesis, informed by the literature median and its heterogeneity. It is not a site-specific forecast. Jordan et al., 2016.
The PEM hypothesis scales specific electricity with 4.8 mV per 1,000 operating hours at 1.9 V, using DOE’s reported 2022 continuous-operation status. Dynamic duty, start damage, thermal cycling and the whole measurement chain remain uncalibrated. Beyond the 10% reference criterion, the experiment is explicitly extrapolative. DOE PEM technical targets.
Rate/duration, missing observations, unsuccessful work, support outages, lower power/storage and additional CO₂ are declared stress scenarios. Bundled changes do not isolate an individual parameter’s causal effect, and the scenario set has no assigned probability distribution.
A low-power test cannot establish full capacity
The controlled-load experiment uses production physics and the real observation/diagnosis interfaces. A 450 kW and a 225 kW electrolyser give identical observations while the requests remain at or below 225 kW. When load exceeds that common feasible region, the shortfall becomes informative. After repair, repeated 180 kW probes support 180 kW; successful upward probes can support progressively more.
All six zero/noisy seeded controlled examples preserve that distinction. They are identifiability demonstrations, not estimates of field detection rates. More logging cannot resolve a physically uninformative test. Reserve enough power and buffer headroom for a meaningful probe, or retain uncertainty and escalate. Recorded controlled-load evidence.


Old experiments remain evidence for their old source
The six stage-3 programmes contain 702 original-source numerical repetitions. Inputs, applied dispatch, reported outcomes and event summaries match their original publications. This closes the provision and interface preservation work without rewriting earlier source, weather, findings or paused-history records.
Each portable export is restored into a temporary directory and checked with the captured standalone checker under isolated Python, without third-party packages or network access. The original ZIP and verification receipt are retained; the redundant temporary extraction is removed. Matching does not claim byte-identical solver plans or every intermediate state, and it does not qualify Release 2’s new mechanics.

Independent calculations check electrical, material and thermal balances, availability, lifecycle clocks, delayed observations, stock, expenses and checkpoint continuity. The Sites checker does not independently reconstruct every legacy service mission; those mechanics have their own production audits, tests and preserved studies. Bounded formal checks cover their declared state models, not the entire lifecycle or a real plant.
The new 72-hour lifecycle bundle has a separate offline check and captured-source numerical repeat. The current-source completion gate above determines whether these checks have finished; the linked receipt records dispatch differences. Original documentation and saved examples are readable offline; live learning-example recalculation needs the restored application. Restoration receipt.
The controlled 240-hour, single-batch interaction fixture passes the 200 ms input and 10 ms render limits. A separate run with the release numerical programme and three archive exporters also active missed the solar input target: 271 ms p95. That stress result is retained; it motivates explicit background resource budgets, not a relaxed interaction target.
Automated checks establish properties of this implementation and its fixtures. They do not establish empirical calibration, hazardous-area suitability, equipment compatibility, certified fuel or real-world autonomous recovery. No overall trust score combines those different claims.

Use the new layer when the question needs it
  1. Open Dispatch Lab, reveal Sites, select an environment and open a design.
  2. Reveal Deployment and maintenance. Inspect the illustrative preset or edit the structured assumptions, then save a new design.
  3. Run or open a saved study. Inspect plant operation at an acceptance event, a maintenance interval or an unconfirmed recovery.
  4. Use Commissioning record or Condition & maintenance in the component inspector. This run shows original information; the Model essays use separate learning fixtures.
  5. Compare multiple boundaries, inspect the source and remaining obligations, then open the saved write-up or portable bundle.
Entering Model pauses playback; Back/Escape restores the originating context and focus. Essays, resets, cancellation, narrow screens and reduced motion have explicit checks. The comprehension walkthrough records agent findings separately from tests. Actual participant comprehension remains unmeasured.


Release 3: learn only within a controlled comparison
Release 2 supplies the deployment, condition, support and evidence contracts that a learned controller must respect. The next release should proceed through the following sequence.
  1. Freeze observation-only datasets and evaluation splits. Register observations, actions, delays, missing channels, prices and source/configuration identities. Keep retrospective truth available to scorers, separate from policy inputs. Hold out weather windows, equipment assumptions and plant sizes before training.
  2. Start with estimators and planning aids. Compare fixed, adaptive and learned estimates of condition, soiling, task duration or continuation value. Test uncertainty and decision consequences, not just prediction error. Include cases with insufficient excitation and failed procedures.
  3. Provide bounded policy deployment. Version trained models and training protocols. Preserve execution limits, solver budgets, fallback and original decision assumptions. Training is separate from interactive playback and never silently changes a published policy.
  4. Evaluate scheduling and homeostatic reserves. Compare production/value objectives with mode-dependent reserves for energy, feedstock, service energy, references, spare parts and unfinished work. Penalise unnecessary stock hoarding, repeated failed interventions and human burden. A controller must earn any improvement over simpler rules.
  5. Publish held-out successes, failures and reversals. Separate numerical repeats, sensor seeds and environmental samples. Report data requirements, training/runtime cost, uncertainty and constraints explaining the result. More elaborate learning need not win.
  6. Qualify the complete research workflow. Finish fresh-install demonstration, numerical resumption, offline recovery, artifact durability, performance and actual participant comprehension across Sites → design → operation → investigation → comparison → write-up.
In parallel, obtain equipment-specific capability and isolation evidence, condition-channel observations, thermal and degradation data, service/logistics exposure and dated quotations. Those inputs can change the model structure or reverse a comparison. Software repeatability cannot supply them.
No learned policy, real-plant interface, certification process, wallet, token, marketplace or settlement has been added in this release. Full three-release roadmap · Release-3 delivery gates.
